newsitem.title: CONGO: Zaire talks delayed, South Africa blames Kabila.
newsitem.headline: Zaire talks delayed, South Africa blames Kabila.

text.p: Rebel leader Laurent Kabila kept South Africa's Nelson Mandela and Zaire's embattled President Mobutu Sese Seko waiting for a second time on Wednesday, delaying crunch peace talks, probably by a day.

Kabila, who kept the two leaders waiting before his first face-to-face meeting with Mobutu on May 4, failed to show again on Wednesday, to the evident irritation of his South African hosts. His aides cited security concerns.

Mandela, who is trying to broker a deal to avert a battle for Zaire's capital Kinshasa, remained in Congo's port of Pointe Noire where the South African icebreaker Outeniqua, venue for the talks, was moored. Mobutu also stayed in Pointe Noire.
"We are still continuing discussions," South African Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad told reporters. "I think we can predict it will start tomorrow."

A spokesman for the rebels said said there would be no talks with President Mobutu Sese Seko on Thursday if the location was Congo's Point Noire port and insisted talks be held in international waters.

"We are not going to have the talks in Point Noire and apparently Mr Mobutu doesn't want to go to the international waters so the talks will not talk place today (Wednesday) or tomorrow," rebel Justice "Commissioner-General" Mwenze Kongolo told Reuters by telephone.
In Kinshasa, a stay-home protest called by the anti-Mobutu opposition all but closed down the usually teeming city of five million people. Shops and markets stayed closed.

"The success of today's operation has clearly shown that the people don't want Mobutu any more, and people know exactly what to do when the rebels come," said Laurent Mbayo, an adviser to Mobutu's veteran political opponent Etienne Tshisekedi.
Zairean state radio had said that Wednesday would be a fateful day that could determine the future of Africa's third largest and potentially one of its richest countries.
South Africa's deputy president, Thabo Mbeki, has billed the talks as a likely last chance for peace.

Mobutu agreed at the first meeting on May 4 to hand power to an elected president. Kabila, both then and in public statements since, has insisted Mobutu hand power at once to his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire.

Mandela spokesman Joel Netshitenzhe said on the eve of the talks that mediators had won agreement in a number of areas. "They have a skeleton of the main areas of agreement that are supposed to be ratified," he told Reuters.
Rebel radio suggested that Kabila's forces were nearing the approaches to Kinshasa. The government dismissed such reports.
Just in case, several thousand Western soldiers remained on standby in Congo's capital Brazzaville or at sea off Zaire to evacuate foreign nationals from Kinshasa if need be.

Mobutu, 66 and suffering from cancer, has dominated Zaire since seizing power in 1965, reputedly amassing a huge personal fortune. Western powers supported him as a Cold War bastion against Soviet communism.
The rebels, who took up arms in October demanding Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis, now control three-quarters of the impoverished, corruption-plagued nation.
Zairean state television, in its main afternoon bulletin, quoted the government as saying that fighting was going on in and around Kenge, more than 200 km (125 miles) from Kinshasa.

It said the Kwango River Bridge, about 180 km (110 miles) by road from the capital, was still in the hands of Mobutu forces. Rebels and Kinshasa residents in contact with the area said earlier it had been abandoned by the army on Monday.
Switzerland said it was examining a request from the interim public prosecutor in the rebel-controlled Zairean city of Lumumbashi for Mobutu's assets in Swiss banks to be frozen.
